## Executive Summary

Black Swift Technologies conducted a Phase I feasibility study to modify the BST S0 unmanned aerial system (UAS) for integration into the Navy's P-8A Poseidon aircraft as an expendable sonobuoy-launched asset supporting anti-submarine warfare (ASW) operations. The research established technical feasibility for integrating a high-sensitivity magnetometer (QuSpin QTFM Gen-2), deployable passive acoustic hydrophone sensor, and AI compute module (NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin) within strict Size, Weight, and Power (SWaP) constraints of a standard LAU-126A Sonobuoy Launch Container (SLC). Ground and flight testing demonstrated that the platform's magnetic noise floor is manageable at five-foot separation distance, achieving 1.5 pT/√Hz—below the Navy's 20 pT/√Hz threshold—while maintaining total system weight under the 39-pound maximum.

## Technical Approach

### Core Methodology
- **Systems Engineering Focus:** Integration of commercial-off-the-shelf (COTS) sensing technologies into the existing S0 platform to meet SWaP-C requirements
- **Test-Heavy Approach:** Spectral density analysis to characterize magnetic noise floor relative to Navy thresholds; ground and flight testing to validate assumptions
- **Dual-Aircraft Architecture:** Program decision to split magnetic and acoustic sensing into two separate S0 variants to maximize mission flexibility and sensor performance

### Key Design Decisions
1. **Magnetometer Integration:** QuSpin QTFM Gen-2 mounted on extendable nose boom to achieve 5-foot separation from electric motor, with optional MuMetal magnetic shielding around motor
2. **Acoustic Subsystem:** Collaboration with Ultra Maritime (replacing initial Cetacean Research Technology partnership) and Cetacean Research Technology to design lightweight hydrophone with independent battery power and fiber-optic tether transmission
3. **Compute Architecture:** NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin 64GB for edge processing and machine learning, integrated with existing S0 avionics
4. **Platform Modifications:** Modified battery using pouch cells (reduced magnetic interference), widened fuselage, extendable boom design, water-sealed avionics compartment with foam buoyancy layer

## Products & Capabilities Described

### S0 Air-Deployed UAS (Modified Variants)

**S0-MAD Variant (Magnetometer Aircraft)**
- Integrates QuSpin QTFM Gen-2 magnetometer on nose boom
- Houses NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin compute module in widened fuselage
- Modified pouch-cell battery to reduce electromagnetic interference
- Specifications:
  - Cruise speed: 70 knots (modified from 50 knots baseline)
  - Endurance: 120 minutes (exceeds 70-minute Navy requirement)
  - Operational altitude: 50–2,000 ft
  - Range: 20 nm LOS (extending to 50 nm with modification)
  - Weight: 15.6 lbs base platform; total system under 39 lb requirement
  - Stowed dimensions: 4.875 in. diameter × 36 in. length (fits LAU-126A SLC)
  - Payload volume: >94.4 cubic inches
  - Operational life: 5 years shelf life (objective: 9 years)

**S0-Acoustic Variant (Hydrophone Aircraft)**
- Designed for controlled water landing and hydrophone deployment
- Houses UM multi-sensor acoustic payload (hydrophone + E-field sensors)
- Water-sealed, foam-buoyed avionics compartment
- Stores 200-foot fiber-optic tethered hydrophone assembly beneath wing pivot
- Uses frangible belly deployment mechanism

### Sensor Payloads

**QuSpin QTFM Gen-2 Magnetometer**
- **Performance:** 3 pT/√Hz in-air noise level (exceeds Navy requirement of 20 pT/√Hz)
- **Measurement bandwidth:** 500 Hz (exceeds 100 Hz requirement)
- **Range:** ±150 μT (exceeds 100 μT requirement)
- **Heading error:** <3 nT uncompensated
- **Operating temperature:** -15°C to 55°C (exceeds -20°C to 50°C requirement)
- **Physical specs:** Sensor head 17.7 × 19.8 × 35.8 mm (12 g), ECU housing 14.7 × 24.4 × 92.3 mm (29 g)
- **Power consumption:** 2.5 W nominal, 3.5 W during startup

**Ultra Maritime Acoustic Sensor Suite**
- **Acoustic frequency coverage:** 5 Hz – 40 kHz (omnidirectional hydrophone)
- **E-field frequency coverage:** 0.01 Hz – 5 Hz (two pairs of ULF and ELFE probes)
- **Hydrophone design:** Acceleration-cancelling design with very low noise preamplifier (10+ dB below Q53H CO specification; 6-8 dB improvement possible with textured ceramic)
- **Operating depth:** 200 ft threshold (400 ft objective)
- **Deployment time:** 120 seconds gravity-based (60 seconds objective)
- **Operating life:** 60 minutes threshold, 70 minutes objective
- **Sensor calibration accuracy:** ±2 dB threshold (±1 dB objective)
- **Detection range:** 20 nm LOS (50 nm objective with increased RF power)
- **Physical packaging:** 4-inch diameter × 6.5-inch length (81.7 cubic inches), with suspension system to reduce mechanically-induced noise
- **Power consumption:** <2.5 W for acoustic sensor; ~5 W with RF communications

**NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin 64GB Compute Module**
- **AI Performance:** 275 TOPS (meets Navy requirement)
- **GPU:** 2048-core with 64 Tensor cores, max frequency 1.3 GHz
- **CPU:** 12-core @ 2.2 GHz
- **Memory:** 64 GB RAM
- **Power consumption:** 15 W – 60 W
- **Physical dimensions:** 110 mm × 110 mm × 71.65 mm
- **Function:** Edge processing, machine learning-based submarine detection/classification, onboard data fusion

### Command & Control
- **SwiftPilot:** Existing BST command and control system; planned extension to UAS Control Segment (UCS) architecture in Phase II
- **Autonomous capabilities:** Pre-programmed waypoint tracks, autonomous target cueing hooks (tested in non-MAD variants)
- **Control interface:** Portable control tablet

## Use Cases & Applications

### Primary Mission
- **Anti-Submarine Warfare (ASW) for U.S. Navy P-8A Poseidon aircraft**
- Cued search, detection, localization, tracking, and classification of hostile submarines
- Maritime Domain Awareness operations in task force protection scenarios

### Operational Concept
1. Sonobuoy-launched deployment from P-8A Poseidon via LAU-126A launch container
2. Two-aircraft distributed search: S0-MAD performs magnetic anomaly detection on signal-based flight patterns; S0-Acoustic executes controlled water landing and deploys tethered hydrophone
3. Coordinated cueing: MAD detections trigger targeted acoustic deployment; acoustic localizations cue refined MAD search patterns
4. On-board machine learning processes both magnetic and acoustic sensor data for autonomous target classification
5. Automated mission termination with classified data sanitization and platform scuttling

### Extended Applications
- NOAA hurricane operations (existing S0 operational use)
- Air Force use cases (noted as expansion target)
- Volcanic and geological monitoring (implied by broader platform capabilities)

## Key Results

### B.1: Requirements Analysis and Preliminary Design

**Component Selection Validation:**
- QuSpin QTFM Gen-2 meets all Navy magnetometer specifications with margin
- NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin selected for 275 TOPS AI performance and sufficient compute density; despite being largest internal component, confirmed to fit within S0 launch tube
- Acoustic hydrophone design feasibility confirmed through collaboration with industry expert (Ultra Maritime)

**Integration Feasibility:**
- S0 platform inherently compatible with SLC constraints; total package weight 15.6 lbs (well under 39 lb maximum)
- Payload volume of modified S0 exceeds 94.4 cubic inch requirement
- 200-foot fiber-optic tethered hydrophone assembly can be stored within aft fuselage compartment

### B.2: Platform Modifications

**Mechanical Compatibility:**
- Folded S0 airframe with deployment tube closely matches weight, size, and center of gravity of existing 36B BT expendable assets
- Ensures identical launch dynamics to current sonobuoy operations; >30 drops through P-3 free-fall chute without separation issues
- Full SLUAV system meets MIL-L-81745B loading specification (~10G for 100ms)

**Design Modifications Completed:**
- Battery redesigned with pouch cells to reduce electromagnetic interference from steel cases
- Fuselage widened underneath wing to accommodate Jetson SBC and maximize motor-sensor separation
- Extendable nose boom design for magnetometer mounting at optimal 5-foot separation
- S0-Acoustic variant includes water-sealed, foam-buoyed avionics compartment and frangible belly deployment mechanism for 200-foot hydrophone assembly

### B.3: Sensor Integration and Testing

#### Magnetometer Testing Results

**S1 Flight Testing (Surrogate Platform):**
- Identified significant heading error (120–150 nT) and high-frequency aliasing from motor throttling
- Platform noise measured at 250–600 pT/√Hz (10–30x requirements), attributed to proximity of larger S1 motor
- Aliasing identified as primary issue (filters ineffective); motor shielding previously demonstrated 10x noise reduction

**S0 Ground Testing (Primary Platform):**
- **Distance-dependent measurements (RMS and spectral density analysis):**
  - 50 ft: 1.5 pT/√Hz (meets requirement)
  - 20 ft: 1.4 pT/√Hz (meets requirement)
  - 10 ft: 1.4 pT/√Hz (meets requirement)
  - **5 ft: 1.4 pT/√Hz – twice as good as 20 pT/√Hz requirement**, providing design margin
  - 0 ft: 34.9 pT/√Hz (exceeds requirement due to proximity)

- **Frequency analysis:**
  - Full frequency range (0–100 Hz) stays below Navy threshold except at 60 Hz (expected from ground-based power line noise)
  - At 5-foot and 2.5-foot distances: no throttle-induced noise visible
  - 400 MHz communications antenna noise detected at 0 and 2.5 ft; antenna relocated to >2.5 ft in updated CAD

- **Key Finding:** 5-foot nose boom separation provides acceptable magnetometer placement without requiring towed sensor design or additional shielding; 2.5-foot separation also viable with updated antenna placement

**Shielding Development:**
- MuMetal magnetic shielding material sourced and prototyped around S0 motor
- Prototype demonstrates feasibility; reserved for Phase II testing if required or for enhanced performance

**Calibration Strategy:**

## Executive Summary
Black Swift Technologies proposes to design, develop, and validate a modular, open-architecture avionics system and cost-effective demonstrator aircraft for advanced multi-vehicle cooperative algorithm research and swarming operations. Building on the proven SwiftCore FMS and S0 platform, this effort will create a turn-key capability enabling coordinated UAS missions in extreme environments while addressing the USAF's strategic need for large numbers of collaborative systems providing synergistic and multidomain effects.

## Technical Approach

**Core Architecture:**
- Leverage BST's SwiftCore Flight Management System—one of the only truly modular autopilot systems with proven performance in extreme environments
- Design an open, modular architecture with well-defined interfaces to enable rapid development and adaptation of cooperative control algorithms
- Develop inexpensive yet capable small UAS demonstrator platforms with networked command and control
- Establish open interfaces and modular design in partnership with AFRL researchers

**Demonstrator Platform:**
- Based on BST's VTOL S0 and air-deployable S0 variants
- Original S0 developed under NOAA SBIR for low-cost, air-deployed hurricane monitoring
- Extended with USAF support to create land-based VTOL variant with vertical takeoff/landing capability
- Includes unique flush-air system embedded in nose cone measuring 3D inertial winds, pressure, temperature, and humidity

**Sensor Capabilities:**
- Well-characterized sensor suite for accurate atmospheric measurements
- EO/IR imagery collection
- 3D wind measurement and meteorological data collection
- Designed for extreme environment operation

## Products & Capabilities Described

### SwiftCore Flight Management System (FMS)
- **What it is:** Modular, ground-up avionics and flight management system with well-defined interfaces
- **Capabilities:** Handles avionics, communications, ground station, and UI in modular fashion
- **Proven in:** Extreme environments with NOAA and NASA
- **Application in proposal:** Foundation for open-architecture cooperative control platform; enables development of advanced multi-vehicle algorithms and simulations across wide variety of USAF platforms

### SwiftPilot FMS
- Extremely capable autopilot system developed from ground up by BST
- Integrated into SwiftCore ecosystem

### S0 UAS Platform
- **Variants:** Air-deployable (NOAA version) and VTOL land-based (USAF version)
- **Original development:** NOAA SBIR for P-3 based hurricane monitoring
- **Extension:** USAF-supported development of VTOL variant for simplified operations
- **Sensors:** Integrated flush-air system for 3D inertial winds, pressure, temperature, humidity measurement
- **Proposed use:** Swarming demonstrator platform base; capable of cooperative missions in extreme conditions

### S2 Aircraft
- Developed from soil moisture mapping SBIR
- Selected for NASA MALIBU (Multi-AngLe Imaging Bidirectional Reflectance Distribution Function UAS) project
- Operational with JPL in Costa Rica for ELEVATE project (trace gas sensing)
- Larger payload capacity (>5 lbs)
- Extended flight times and range vs. multi-rotors

## Executive Summary
This SBIR solicitation calls for the development of a small, low-cost unmanned aircraft system (UAS) designed specifically for atmospheric sampling with high autonomy and ease of operation. The system must measure wind velocity, pressure, temperature, and humidity while being capable of autonomous flight, rapid deployment by a single operator, and accommodation of additional sensor payloads.

## Technical Approach

**Phase I - Design and Requirements Development:**
- Develop conceptual models, functional requirements, and component architectures
- Select or design airframe with capability for:
  - Fully autonomous flight including take-off and landing
  - Rapid assembly and deployment by single operator
  - Ruggedized construction for unimproved surfaces
- Design avionics system including:
  - Atmospheric sensor suite selection
  - Autopilot system interfaces
  - Multi-aircraft user interface for mission execution and monitoring
  - Autonomous sampling algorithms
- Develop test plan to experimentally validate sensing systems

**Phase II - Prototype Development and Validation:**
- Build and demonstrate functional prototype
- Implement and test autonomous sampling algorithms
- Gain airspace access and conduct atmospheric data validation experiments

**Phase III - Commercialization:**
- Prepare software, hardware, and documentation for commercial release

## Key Parameters & Requirements
- **Primary measurements:** Wind velocity, pressure, temperature, humidity
- **Operational requirements:** Low cost, easy to operate, high autonomy
- **Deployment:** Single operator capable, rapid assembly
- **Airframe:** Ruggedized for unimproved surfaces, autonomous capable
- **Interface:** Multi-aircraft simultaneous control capability
- **Payload flexibility:** Designed to accommodate additional sensors (particulate detection/classification)

## Use Cases & Applications
- Atmospheric sampling and meteorological measurements
- Wind velocity profiling
- Environmental monitoring with expandable sensor suites

## References
- SUMO
- DataHawk
- V2 Paper
- Multi-holed probe

- This document is a solicitation topic description rather than a BST proposal response or report

## Executive Summary
This letter of support endorses Black Swift Technologies' Phase II SBIR proposal for developing an expendable, sonobuoy-launched unmanned aerial vehicle equipped with Magnetic Anomaly Detection (MAD) and passive acoustic sensors for Anti-Submarine Warfare (ASW) operations. The letter confirms successful Phase I completion and commits unnamed technology partner support for Phase II prototype fabrication and validation.

## Technical Approach
- Integration of high-sensitivity payloads (MAD and passive acoustic sensors) into BST's S0 platform
- Design adherence to strict Size, Weight, and Power (SWaP) constraints of the LAU-126A Sonobuoy Launch Container
- Magnetic noise reduction through:
  - Magnetic shielding
  - Boom extension
- Edge processing via NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin

## Products & Capabilities Described

**S0 Platform**
- Expendable sonobuoy-launched UAV
- Capable of accommodating high-sensitivity payloads within LAU-126A container constraints
- Platform-induced magnetic noise floor: ~1.5 pT/√Hz at 5 feet separation (Phase I result)
- Meets Navy threshold requirement for magnetic noise
- Proposed to enable ASW target detection, tracking, and classification

**Sensors**
- Magnetic Anomaly Detection (MAD) sensor (specific model not named)
- Passive acoustic sensors (likely QuSpin QTFM Gen-2 and CRT Hydrophone based on bracketed examples)
- NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin for edge signal processing

## Use Cases & Applications
- Anti-Submarine Warfare (ASW) operations
- Cued search, detection, tracking, and classification of submarines
- Naval operations using sonobuoy launch platforms

## Key Results (Phase I)
- Feasibility of integrating MAD and passive acoustic sensors into S0 platform established
- Magnetic noise characterization: ~1.5 pT/√Hz at 5 feet separation distance
- Successfully demonstrated compatibility with LAU-126A Sonobuoy Launch Container SWaP requirements
- Performance met Navy threshold requirements

## Document Metadata
- Type: Peer-reviewed journal article / research report
- Client/Agency: NASA / Pioneer Venus Working Group
- Program/Solicitation: Pioneer Venus mission results
- Date: December 30, 1980
- BST Products/Systems Referenced: None
- Key Personnel: None (BST connection: Document filed in BST's 2018 SBIR Venus Phase I proposal reference materials; indexed by Jack Elston)

## Executive Summary
This comprehensive analysis of Pioneer Venus mission data presents findings on the thermal structure, circulation patterns, and dynamics of Venus's atmosphere across multiple altitude regimes (surface to 100+ km). The study reveals unexpected horizontal temperature contrasts, strong zonal retrograde winds (~100 m/s at cloud tops), a complex meridional circulation including a cloud-level Hadley cell, and evidence of eddy contributions throughout the atmosphere.

## Technical Approach
Multi-instrument analysis combining data from:
- **Pioneer Venus entry probes** (4 probes at different latitudes/local times): temperature, pressure, wind measurements via Differential Long-Baseline Interferometry (DLBI) and Doppler tracking
- **Pioneer Venus orbiter**: radio occultation measurements, Orbiter Infrared Radiometer (OIR) temperature retrievals, Orbiter Cloud Photopolarimeter (OCPP) cloud tracking
- **Venera probes** (Soviet): complementary atmospheric measurements
- **Historical data**: Mariner 10 ultraviolet observations

## Key Findings by Altitude Regime

### Surface to 28 km (Deep Atmosphere)
- **Temperature contrasts**: 1-2% horizontal variations (larger than pre-mission predictions of <0.1 K)
- **Latitudinal differences**: ~5 K contrasts observed between equatorial and polar locations
- **Vertical structure**: Nearly adiabatic layer (20-30 km); stable layer below 16-18 km at equatorial latitudes; neutral stability at 60°N extending to 12 km
- **Zonal winds**: Westward (retrograde), sluggish below 7 km (~1 m/s), reaching ~30 m/s at 28 km
- **Wind shear**: Alternating high/low shear layers at low latitudes correlate with static stability variations; monotonically increasing shear at high latitudes
- **Meridional winds**: <2 m/s, variable in direction; no clear mean Hadley cell signature
- **Key conclusion**: Eddies contribute significantly; pure Hadley circulation model insufficient to explain observations

### 28-65 km (Cloud Region)
- **Dominant feature**: Strong retrograde (westward) zonal circulation with winds increasing monotonically from near-zero at 10 km to ~100 m/s at 60-70 km
- **Static stability**: Stable below ~50 km; nearly adiabatic layer within clouds (50-55 km); sharp temperature inversion ("tropopause") at ~100 mbar pressure level
- **Latitudinal temperature gradient**: Increases with altitude above 28 km; north probe consistently coolest
- **Meridional circulation**: 
  - Below 40 km: variable, no coherent pattern
  - 50-55 km: equatorward winds at all probes (~5-10 m/s)
  - Cloud-tracked ultraviolet observations: poleward meridional motion (~several m/s)
  - **Interpretation**: Cloud-level Hadley cell with rising equatorial branch and poleward/descending polar branch forming a polar vortex
- **Cyclostrophic balance**: Zonal winds above 40 km maintained in approximate balance with meridional pressure gradients
- **Angular momentum**: Peak at ~20 km altitude; decreases poleward, suggesting poleward transport by Hadley cell
- **Richardson number**: Generally >>1 (stable); shear instability only in neutral cloud layer
- **Temporal variability**: Evidence from CO₂ spectroscopic measurements and Venera comparisons suggests ±50% variations in zonal wind speeds over time
- **Polar features**: OIR observations show wavenumber-2 eddies (180° separation) rotating about pole with 2.7-day period

### 65-100 km (Upper Cloud to Homopause Region)
- **Temperature structure**: 
  - 70-95 km shows reversed latitudinal gradient (warm pole, cool equator) - unexpected and not fully explained
  - High variability above 80 km in time and space (~25 K daily changes)
  - Sharp temperature inversion 62-70 km at 60° latitude (long-lived, at least 62+ days)
- **Zonal winds**: Cloud-tracked winds ~100 m/s; heterodyne measurements suggest winds persist to 70-80 km altitude
- **Proposed mechanisms for polar warming**: 
  - Poleward mean meridional circulation with adiabatic compression
  - Diabatic heating from polar cloud clearing allowing infrared penetration
  - Submicron polar haze with near-infrared absorption
  - Planetary-scale wave transport of heat from lower atmosphere
- **Uncertainties**: Direction of meridional circulation above 60 km unclear; no obvious diabatic heating mechanism definitively identified

### Above 100 km (Upper Atmosphere)
- **Thermal structure**: Marked day/night asymmetry
  - **Day side**: Thermosphere with temperatures increasing to exospheric ~300 K
  - **Night side**: "Cryosphere" with temperatures decreasing to exospheric ~100 K
- **Superrotation**: Atmospheric superrotation observed at 150+ km altitudes
- **Circulation**: Subsolar-to-antisolar flow (100 m/s) near 115 km altitude

## Eddy Phenomena
Evidence throughout atmosphere:
- **Small-scale gravity waves**: Throughout atmosphere
- **Convective cells**: Particularly in neutral cloud layer (50-55 km)
- **Planetary-scale waves**: Wavenumber 1 (tracking of cloud features), wavenumber 2 at poles (2.7-day rotation)
- **Barotropic instability**: Suggested by temporal variations in Mariner 10 vs. Pioneer Venus wind profiles
- **Role in transport**: Eddies and mean meridional circulation both important for energy and momentum redistribution

## Major Discoveries vs. Pre-Mission Expectations

| Aspect | Pre-Mission Model | Actual Observations |
|--------|------------------|-------------------|
| Horizontal thermal contrasts | <0.1 K | 1-15 K measured |
| Longitudinal variation | Negligible | 5 K at some levels |
| Deep atmosphere stability | Nearly neutral | Stable layers present |
| Meridional Hadley cell | Efficient redistribution | Weak/uncertain below clouds; clear above |
| Wind structure | Smooth profile | Layered shear structure |
| Cloud-level circulation | Unknown | ~100 m/s retrograde with poleward Hadley cell |
| Polar upper atmosphere | Cool | Anomalously warm (reversed gradient) |

## Notable Technical Details

### Measurement Limitations Acknowledged
- Probes sampled single locations at single time instants
- Most entries near morning terminator; only 1 at night, 1 poleward of 33°; none in late afternoon/evening
- Probe data cannot separate temporal/zonal averages from eddy contributions
- Venera data (subsolar region) has large published uncertainties (±4.2-8.5 K temperature, ±2 km altitude)

### Temporal Variability Evidence
- CO₂ absorption line spectroscopy: ±50% zonal wind variations
- Mariner 10 vs. Pioneer Venus cloud-tracked winds: suggest real time-dependent changes
- 4-day rotation period observed sporadically over long periods (established as real mass motion, not wave phenomenon)
- Occultation measurements separated by 61-72 days show large differences in upper atmosphere

### Angular Momentum Conservation
- Cloud-tracked observations: Angular momentum conserved from equator to ±45° (Mariner 10 data)
- Pioneer Venus OCPP: Suggests constant angular velocity instead
- DLBI profiles: Wind speed increases with latitude 30-60 km, decreases below 30 km
- Discrepancies attributed to temporal variability in zonal wind field

## Unresolved Questions
1. **Mechanism maintaining zonal circulation**: Eddies vs. mean meridional circulation vs. waves—not definitively established
2. **Stable layer in deep atmosphere**: Difficult to reconcile with radiative equilibrium and Hadley cell models; would require decreased opacity/water vapor near surface
3. **Polar stratospheric warming**: No single mechanism definitively explains reversed latitudinal temperature gradient 70-95 km
4. **Layered wind/shear structure**: Physical mechanism for alternating high/low shear layers not identified
5. **Energy balance**: Observed net infrared upward fluxes exceed downward solar flux in lower atmosphere, raising question of downward heat transport by dynamics

## Broader Implications
- Venus's atmospheric circulation is **not steady** despite small obliquity and nearly circular orbit—evidence of temporal variability
- **Eddies and small-scale features** appear to be essential components, not just perturbations
- **Separation of circulations**: Strongly stable layer below clouds (~45 km) may decouple lower and upper atmosphere dynamics
- **Comparison to Earth**: Reversed polar stratospheric gradients known in Earth's upper atmosphere; may be general phenomenon in stably-stratified atmospheres with strong zonal flow

## Document Context for BST
This reference was compiled for Black Swift Technologies' 2018 SBIR Phase I proposal on **Venus atmospheric measurements**. The document provides comprehensive baseline scientific understanding of Venus atmospheric structure and dynamics that would inform mission requirements, scientific payload design, and operational strategies for aerial platform operations in Venus's atmosphere.# Using Small Uncrewed Aircraft Systems to Mitigate Post-Landfall Hurricane Disasters

## Executive Summary
This document proposes using Black Swift's small, electric S0 unmanned aircraft system to collect high-value post-landfall hurricane data in real-time for emergency response teams. A consortium of federal, academic, and private partners would deploy the S0 from shoreline locations immediately after hurricane landfall to gather atmospheric and imagery data for damage assessment and civil infrastructure evaluation.

## Technical Approach
- Deployment of Black Swift S0 aircraft from shoreline immediately after landfall when winds have subsided
- Operation under FAA Part 107 regulations (initially line-of-sight, under 400 ft AGL)
- Aircraft equipped with selectable sensor suites for atmospheric measurements or electro-optical/infrared imagery
- Automated flight processes for area-of-interest identification and coverage planning
- Video telemetry to ground station with geo-referencing for post-processing into orthomosaics and 3D models
- Real-time data relay through existing NOAA and emergency management channels
- Future advancement to Beyond Visual Line of Sight (BVLOS) and higher altitude operations

## Products & Capabilities Described

### Black Swift S0
- **What it is:** Small electric, modular, ruggedized VTOL (vertical takeoff/landing) or tube-launched fixed-wing unmanned aircraft system compliant with FAA Part 107
- **Specifications:**
  - Maximum takeoff weight: 4 lbs
  - Wingspan: 54.6 inches
  - Payload capacity: 100 grams
  - Flight ceiling: 15,000 ft
  - Flight time: 60 minutes nominal
  - Cruise speed: 40 mph
  - Max speed: 100 mph
  - Max winds endured: 50 mph
  - Nose cone: 1.8 inch diameter
- **Proposed Use:** Real-time post-hurricane data collection for emergency response and damage assessment
- **Sensor Options:** 
  1. 3D wind, pressure, temperature, humidity (atmospheric thermodynamic package)
  2. Electro-optical/infrared (EO/IR) imagery
  3. Trace gas sensors (future capability)
- **Advantages:** Modern manufacturing techniques enable economical construction, operation, and maintenance relative to manned or larger UAS; designed for low-cost solutions including scenarios where aircraft may not be recovered

## Use Cases & Applications
- **Primary Use Case:** Post-landfall hurricane damage assessment
- **Specific Applications:**
  - Real-time surface wind field data collection
  - Civil infrastructure damage assessment
  - Coastal and ecological system impact evaluation
  - Supporting first responders and emergency management teams
  - Atmospheric profiling in hurricane-affected areas
- **Geographic Context:** Landfalling hurricanes along U.S. coastline

## Operational Context
- University of Florida team has deployed sensors in nearly 40 landfalling tropical cyclones (including 10+ major hurricanes) since 1999
- UF team positioned in hurricane core at landfall for immediate post-storm deployment within hours of inland movement
- Established relationships with operational users (NOAA, FEMA) and research agencies (NSF, NIST) for rapid data dissemination

## Notable Details
- **Regulatory Strategy:** Document notes intention to initially operate under Part 107 (no formal FAA approval required) while later seeking BVLOS and above-400-ft authority
- **Consortium Model:** Partnership approach across federal (NOAA), academic (UF, Embry Riddle), and private sector (Black Swift, Lone Star UAS Center) organizations
- **Data Sharing Strategy:** Real-time processed imagery, video, and atmospheric data delivered through existing emergency response channels

Not applicable. This is a compliance plan, not a results report.

His current work emphasizes fundamental understanding of aerosol-cloud interactions and radiative forcing mechanisms.# Sensor Payload Overview – NightFOX Project

## Document Metadata
- Type: Technical overview / payload specification document
- Client/Agency: NOAA
- Program/Solicitation: FY17 UASPO (Unmanned Aircraft Systems Program Office); FIREX (Fire and Smoke Research)
- Project Name: NightFOX (Nighttime Fire Observations)
- Date: Created/Modified December 26, 2019
- BST Products/Systems Referenced: 5-hole probe (wind measurement)
- Key Personnel: Jack Elston (last editor), Troy Thornberry and Ru-Shan Gao (payload development leads)

## Executive Summary
NightFOX developed dual sensor payloads (in situ and remote sensing) for small UAS to measure wildfire emissions and characteristics. The in situ package measures CO2, CO, aerosols, and atmospheric conditions with 1-second response time at $10-15K cost. The remote sensing package uses multi-spectral detectors including mid-infrared sensors to map fire extent and measure fire radiative power (FRP) at $15-20K cost.

## Technical Approach

### In Situ Payload Development
- **Sensors included:** CO2, CO, fine-mode aerosols (140-3000 nm), coarse-mode aerosols (1-10 μm), relative humidity, temperature, pressure
- **Wind measurement:** BST 5-hole probe
- **Key requirement:** Achieve 1-second response time (vs. typical 10-60 second commercial sensors) to maintain ~0.5 km spatial resolution at 20 m/s cruise speed
- **Strategy:** Evaluate commercial/OEM CO and CO2 sensors; modify for response time; develop custom sensors where commercial options insufficient (e.g., fine-mode aerosol)
- **Fine-mode aerosol sensor:** Custom instrument previously developed (reference: Gao et al., 2016)
- **Environmental sensors:** InterMet RH/T/p sensors (iMet-XQ)
- **Cost target:** $10-15K per package (~10× cheaper than manned aircraft equivalents)

### Remote Sensing Payload Development
- **Spectral coverage:** Multiple detectors across visible, mid-infrared (MIR, ~4 μm), and long-wavelength infrared (LWIR, 7-14 μm)
- **Primary objectives:** Map fire perimeter and measure fire radiative power (FRP)
- **Technical challenge:** LWIR thermal imagers saturate at fire radiances; MIR imagers costly and bulky
- **Solution:** Single-element 4 μm sensors (small, low-cost) for FRP determination
- **Scanning approach:** Cross-track scanning with narrow field-of-view MIR sensor; visible/thermal cameras for high-resolution context
- **Data management:** Onboard computer for full data storage; real-time subset transmitted to ground for decision-making
- **Cost target:** $15-20K per package

## Products & Capabilities Described

### BST 5-Hole Probe
- **What it is:** Wind measurement probe
- **Application in NightFOX:** Integrated into in situ payload for wind velocity measurements on small UAS
- **Context:** Identified as suitable solution for UAS wind measurement requirements

### Payload Integration
- **Multi-sensor fusion:** Simultaneous in situ and remote sensing measurements from single platform
- **Real-time telemetry:** Subset of sensor data downlinked for operational fire monitoring
- **Data archival:** Full datasets submitted to FIREX data archive

## Use Cases & Applications

**Primary Application:** Nighttime and daytime wildfire characterization

**Specific measurements:**
- Fire combustion efficiency (via CO2/CO ratio analysis)
- Wildfire-produced aerosol characterization (health impact assessment)
- Fire extent mapping
- Fire radiative power distribution
- Ambient atmospheric conditions in fire plumes

**Mission context:** NOAA FIREX campaign; small fixed-wing UAS operations (cruise speed ~20 m/s)

## Development Timeline
- **Year 1:** Laboratory evaluation of candidate sensors and imagers; selection of optimal components
- **Year 2:** Prototype in situ and remote payload integration; custom sensor modifications; test flights on UAS
- **Year 3:** Finalization of both payloads; construction of two spare payloads

## Notable Details

- **SWaP optimization challenge:** Document emphasizes difficulty of reducing size, weight, power, and cost while maintaining research-grade sensor performance for UAS
- **Response time criticality:** Highlights synchronization problem when sensors have different response times; advocates for 1-second standard
- **Commercial sensor limitations:** Identifies insufficient sensitivity and cross-species interferences in industrial solid-state sensors; justifies custom development approach
- **Cost efficiency:** Target of $10-15K in situ package represents ~10× cost reduction vs. manned aircraft instruments without performance loss
- **Partnerships/References:** References InterMet Systems for environmental sensors; cites prior work (Gao et al., 2016) on fine-mode aerosol sensing
- **Sensor redundancy:** Two separate aerosol sensors targeting complementary particle size ranges for comprehensive aerosol characterization

## Document Metadata
- Type: Technical specification/requirements document
- Client/Agency: NASA
- Program/Solicitation: 2018 SBIR - Terrain Following (Phase I)
- Date: 2018-10-01 to 2018-10-08
- BST Products/Systems Referenced: None explicitly (document evaluates sensor options for potential integration)
- Key Personnel: Austin Anderson (commentator)

## Executive Summary
This document evaluates sensor technologies suitable for autonomous terrain-following flight, establishing long-range and short-range obstacle detection requirements and comparing performance, SWaP-C (Size, Weight, Power, Cost), and processing needs across multiple sensor families including cameras, thermal imagers, lidar, radar, and lasers.

## Sensing Architecture
The document establishes a two-tier detection strategy modeled on automotive ADAS systems:
- **Long-range detection**: Coarse detection of large obstacles at distance for early corrective action
- **Short-range detection**: Fine detection of smaller obstacles at close range for terminal collision avoidance

---

## Long-Range Sensor Requirements

| Parameter | Value | Type |
|-----------|-------|------|
| Min Range | 10 m | Minimum |
| Max Range | 100 m | Maximum |
| Obstacle Size | 10 m² | Minimum |
| Obstacle Height | 5 m | Minimum |
| Range Resolution | 50 cm | Minimum |
| Field of View (Az, El) | 45°, 17° | Minimum (TBR) |
| Update Rate | 5 Hz | Minimum |
| Detection Rate | 99.9% | Minimum |

*Note: Internal comments indicate 50m min range was "ludicrously conservative" and FOV values are placeholder estimates requiring review.*

---

## Short-Range Sensor Requirements

| Parameter | Value | Type |
|-----------|-------|------|
| Min Range | 1 m | Minimum |
| Max Range | 20 m | Maximum |
| Obstacle Size | 1 m² | Minimum |
| Obstacle Height | 2 m | Minimum |
| Range Resolution | 5 cm | Minimum |
| Field of View (Az, El) | 60°, 20° | Minimum (TBR) |
| Update Rate | 20 Hz | Minimum |
| Detection Rate | 99% | Minimum |

---

## Products & Capabilities Described

### Single Cameras (Visible Light)

**Characteristics:**
- Small, light, low power consumption
- Require substantial processing for obstacle detection
- Performance highly dependent on visual diversity and lighting conditions

**Performance by Mission Type:**
- **Good performance**: Canopy sampling, mountain sampling, farm sampling (clear weather, good visual diversity), safe landing/takeoff with visual diversity
- **Poor performance**: Arctic/oceanic missions (lack visual diversity), volcanic plumes, fog, heavy rain, snow, icing, water on lens

**Obstacle Performance:**
- Large obstacles (structures, boulders, ridges, wind turbines): easily identified
- Vegetation/trees: detectable in multi-image depth maps
- **Challenge**: Small/thin structures (power lines)

**Processing Requirements:**
- Very high-density processing needed for depth maps and visual odometry
- Image data up to 50 Hz requires USB 3.0, GigE, or PCIe
- Deep learning: requires GPUs or dedicated accelerators with millions of computations per estimate
- Significant RAM and storage for image buffering

**Example Parts & SWaP-C:**

| Part | Size | Weight | Power | Cost |
|------|------|--------|-------|------|
| Ximea MC124CG-SY | 26×26×33 mm | 38g | 3.25 W | $3,055 |
| LI-USB30-C570X | 26×26×38 mm | 32g | 1.12 W | $699 |
| LI-USB30-M021 | 26×26×38 mm | 22g | 0.85 W | $229 |

**Critical Requirements:**
- **Shutter Type**: Global shutter (prevents motion blur critical for odometry/matching; rolling shutter may have higher pixel density but suffers from blur)
- **Focal Length**: Inversely proportional to FOV and stereo range resolution; directly proportional to disparity resolution
- **Field of View**: Wider FOV shows more obstacles and aids digital stabilization, but maps fixed-size obstacles to fewer pixels (harder detection); narrow FOV requires tighter pointing/stabilization
- **Imager Size**: Affects maximum stereo disparity
- **Pixel Count**: Critical for algorithmic performance; dictates minimum realizable disparity and pixel occupancy of objects; scales processing requirements
- **Color vs. Monochromatic**: Monochromatic produces 1/3 data of color; reduces processing if sufficient for task
- **Dynamic Range**: Determines lighting scenario tolerance
- **Frames Per Second**: Higher rates identify obstacles faster but generate more data

**Target Specs:**
- Global shutter
- 2M pixels minimum
- 4.5 µm maximum pixel size
- 50 dB dynamic range (10 bits)
- 5 Hz minimum frame rate
- Color preferred for deep learning
- 5.5 mm focal length, f/1.8 aperture
- 76°/64.5°/51° FOV (D/H/V)
- Max 26×26×33 mm, 50g, 4W, $1,000

---

### Thermal Cameras

**Characteristics:**
- Produces temperature-based imagery
- Lower resolution and limited performance compared to standard cameras
- Simpler processing than visible light (binning sufficient for many tasks)

**Performance by Mission Type:**
- **Good**: Farm mapping (man-made structure identification), populated areas
- Unlikely suitable for odometry/depth mapping

**Obstacle Performance:**
- Excels at detecting warm objects: power lines, humans, man-made structures, vehicles
- Shows contrast against environmental background

**Processing Requirements:**
- Lower resolution (single channel) produces much smaller images than comparably-priced visible cameras
- Simple binning algorithm produces pixel maps of objects of interest
- Simpler identification algorithms than deep learning networks

**Example Parts & SWaP-C:**

| Part | Size | Weight | Power | Cost |
|------|------|--------|-------|------|
| FLIR Lepton | 12.5×12.5×10 mm | 5g | 0.16 W | $239.95 |
| FLIR Duo | 41×59×29.6 mm | 84g | 3.3 W | $1,000 |
| FLIR Duo Pro R | 85×81.3×68.5 mm | 325g | 10 W | $7,600 |

**Target Specs:**
- 4.8k pixels minimum
- 17 µm maximum pixel size
- 40 dB dynamic range (8 bits)
- 5 Hz minimum frame rate
- 5.5 mm focal length, f/1.8 aperture
- 50°/60° FOV (H/D)
- Max 41×60×30 mm, 50g, 4W, $1,000

---

### Stereo Cameras (Visible Light)

**Characteristics:**
- Two synchronized cameras producing simultaneous depth images via visual disparity
- Many commercial systems available with integrated processing accelerators
- Simplified processing compared to single-camera depth mapping but less design flexibility

**Performance:** Same as single cameras

**SWaP-C:**
Smaller and cheaper than single cameras due to widespread mobile robotics use.

**Example Parts & SWaP-C:**

| Part | Size | Weight | Power | Cost |
|------|------|--------|-------|------|
| RealSense D435 | 90×25×25 mm | 72g | 3.5 W | $179 |
| ZED-M | 175×30×30 mm | 159g | 2 W | $449 |
| ZED | 124.5×30.5×26.5 mm | 63g | 2 W | $449 |

**Target Specs:**
- 10 m minimum range
- 10 Hz minimum update rate
- 1280×720 minimum pixels
- 80°×50° FOV (H×V)
- Max 200×40×40 mm, 160g, 4W, $500

**Processing:** Similar to single cameras with baseline requirement for stereo matching

---

### Structured Light Cameras

**Characteristics:**
- Similar to stereo cameras but include active structured light component
- Struggle in bright lighting and inclement weather

**Performance:** Same as single/stereo cameras

**Processing:** Same as stereo cameras

**Example Parts & SWaP-C:**

| Part | Size | Weight | Power | Cost |
|------|------|--------|-------|------|
| RealSense D435 | 90×25×25 mm | 72g | 3.5 W | $179 |

**Target Specs:** Same as stereo cameras

---

### 1D Lasers (Single Point Range Sensors)

**Characteristics:**
- Very accurate, rapid range measurements to fixed points
- Narrow beamwidth leaves large unmapped regions
- Multiple lasers can build sparse point clouds when corrected with IMU

**Performance by Mission Type:**
- **Excellent**: Areas without significant vegetation, farm sampling, mountain sampling, landing/takeoff
- **Challenging**: Canopy sampling (varied range response), arctic/oceanic sampling (snow/water reflectivity dependent), volcanic plumes
- **Weather-independent** (mostly)

**Obstacle Performance:**
- **Excellent**: Solid large obstacles (structures, utility poles, wind turbines, vehicles, boulders, ridge lines)
- **Challenging**: Foliage, dense vegetation, power lines (due to narrow beam width)

**Processing Requirements:**
- Minimal processing (single range measurements)
- Array systems or temporal filtering may require light estimation

**Example Parts & SWaP-C:**

| Part | Size | Weight | Power | Cost |
|------|------|--------|-------|------|
| LightWare LW20/C | 20×30×35 mm | 20g | 0.55 W | $370 |

**Target Specs:**
- 100 m minimum range
- 20 Hz minimum update rate
- 0.2° maximum beamwidth
- Max 20×30×35 mm, 20g, 1W, $400

---

### Lidar (Scanning Laser Rangefinder)

**Characteristics:**
- Single or multi-channel scanning laser producing point clouds
- Works well across most mission scenarios
- Larger, heavier, more expensive than single lasers

**Performance by Mission Type:**
- **Excellent**: All missions except potentially arctic/oceanic (surface reflection), volcanic plumes

**Obstacle Performance:**
- **Excellent**: All obstacle types
- Better than single lasers in canopies (point cloud catches minimum distances across canopy)
- **Excellent**: Power line detection

**Processing Requirements:**
- Point cloud filtering/clustering
- More significant data generation than single lasers
- Requires larger RAM and storage
- Does not require pixel matching or deep learning

**Example Parts & SWaP-C:**

| Part | Size (D/H) | Weight | Power | Cost |
|------|-----------|--------|-------|------|
| Velodyne PUCK VLP-16 | 103/72 mm | 830g | 8 W | $4,000 |
| LightWare SF40/C | 79/91 mm | 270g | 30 W | $1,000 |

**Target Specs:**
- 100 m minimum range
- 5 Hz minimum update rate
- 180° minimum horizontal FOV
- ±10° minimum vertical FOV
- Max 20×30×35 mm, 450g (ideally 225g), 10W typical, $5,000
- Weight is significantly over budget requirement

---

### Radar (Electronically Scanning)

**Characteristics:**
- Rapid volumetric scanning capability
- Works in all weather, day/night
- Can be coarse for fine obstacle avoidance
- May struggle with low-RCS targets and wind turbines (Doppler effects)

**Performance by Mission Type:**
- **Excellent**: All scenarios

**Obstacle Performance:**
- **Excellent**: Large RCS targets at great range
- **Challenging**: Small RCS obstacles (tree branches,# NightFOX SERTC Test Flight After Action Report

## Document Metadata
- Type: Situation Report / After Action Report
- Client/Agency: NOAA ESRL CSD (Earth System Research Laboratory, Chemical Sciences Division)
- Program/Solicitation: NOAA FIREX (Fire and Smoke Study) / NightFOX (Nighttime Fire Observations)
- Date: November 15, 2018 (report date); Test flight: November 8, 2018
- BST Products/Systems Referenced: S2 UAS
- Key Personnel: Ru-Shan Gao (NOAA), Troy Thornberry (NOAA), CU IRISS team (pilots)

## Executive Summary
A test flight of the S2 UAS with remote sensing payload was conducted on November 8, 2018, at SERTC facility in Pueblo, CO, to evaluate nighttime fire observation capabilities for the NightFOX project. While the mission was unable to observe the planned fire due to battery performance issues in cold weather conditions, the flight successfully demonstrated FAA-approved nighttime operations at 2000 ft AGL and validated the S2's lighting systems for night operations.

## Technical Approach
- Integration of remote sensing payload (infrared imaging system for fire detection) onto the S2 UAS
- Nighttime flight operations under FAA Certificate of Authorization (COA) with waiver approval
- Test flight planned at controlled burn site with wooden pallet and hay bale constructed fire
- Maximum authorized altitude: 2000 ft above ground level (still within line of sight)
- Flight conducted in severe cold weather conditions (near 20°F ambient temperature)

## Products & Capabilities Described

### S2 UAS
- Multi-rotor UAS platform modified with lighting systems for nighttime operations
- Capable of carrying remote sensing payloads
- Designed for UAS operations with in situ and remote sensing instruments
- Lighting system described as "clearly visible" and satisfactory for field operations
- Demonstrated ability to reach 2000 ft altitude with operational payload
- Right wing sustained minor damage from frost-related landing (remained flyable)

### Remote Sensing Payload
- Infrared imaging capability for fire/smoke detection
- Integration onto S2 successful based on prior Boulder test flights
- Objective: observe fire temperature and characteristics at night

### In Situ Payload
- Smoke plume sampling capability
- Not deployed in this test; planned for future laboratory fire sampling

## Use Cases & Applications
- Nighttime fire observation and monitoring (NightFOX program)
- Fire and smoke characterization during FIREX-AQ operations (planned for summer)
- Arctic operations and future NOAA ARL deployments

## Key Results

### Successes:
1. **FAA Authorization**: Obtained FAA COA for nighttime operations to 2000 ft AGL with support from Denver Approach
2. **Nighttime Flight Demonstrated**: Successfully conducted nighttime takeoff and landing with S2
3. **Lighting Validation**: S2 lighting systems proved adequate for nighttime operations visibility
4. **Maximum Altitude Achievement**: Reached authorized 2000 ft altitude with operating instrument payload
5. **Institutional Relationship**: Established working relationship with SERTC; future test opportunities planned for April

### Failures/Limitations:
- Fire observation not achieved due to operational constraints
- Smoke plume sampling not conducted
- UAS battery severely degraded by cold temperature (20°F), dropping from full charge to 70% during short flight
- Frost accumulation on aircraft during flight created icing hazard (pitco tube risk)
- Landing skid distance increased due to grass frost, resulting in minor wing damage
- Cancelled further flights due to icing conditions

## Notable Details

**Environmental Challenges:**
- Unexpected low temperatures (near 20°F) with unusually high relative humidity
- Frost formation on grass and aircraft wings during flight
- Brush at facility too damp for self-propagating fire; artificial fire constructed instead

**Operational Constraints:**
- Limited testing window due to: FAA COA/waiver processing time, CU IRISS crew duty time limits, site access legal negotiations, NOAA purchase order processing
- Crew duty time limit caused late afternoon arrival, reducing available test window

**Lessons Learned:**
1. Lighting systems critical for nighttime takeoff and landing safety
2. Adequate crew staffing necessary for desired operational tempo
3. Cold weather battery performance severely compromised; needs further investigation for operational limitation determination (noted as non-issue for FIREX-AQ in August, but important for future projects)

**Future Plans:**
- Advance instruments/payloads from prototype to operational status
- Laboratory fire sampling for in situ payload validation
- Proceed with FIREX-AQ deployment planned for summer operations# Service Agreement - Purchasing Website

## Document Metadata
- Type: Final Report (SF 298 - Report Documentation Page)
- Client/Agency: NASA / Shared Services Center (Stennis Space Center)
- Program/Solicitation: SBIR 2022-1-1118; Contract: 80NSSC22CA192
- Date: 07-08-2024 (Final Report submitted)
- Coverage Period: 08/09/2024 to 08/07/2024
- BST Products/Systems Referenced: Small UAS (uncrewed aircraft systems)
- Key Personnel: Jack Elston, Maciej Stachura, Josh Fromm (all 720-638-9656)

## Executive Summary
This final report documents Black Swift Technologies' SBIR Phase II-e work on developing a ruggedized UAS for scientific data gathering in harsh environments. The project focused on addressing limitations in atmospheric data collection for volcanic ash monitoring and other hazardous atmospheric phenomena by enabling small UAS to operate autonomously in difficult conditions without requiring extensive manual intervention and specialized expertise.

## Technical Approach
BST's approach centered on automating mission planning and flight management for small UAS operations in challenging atmospheric environments:

- **Autonomous Operations Focus**: Development of systems to conduct missions automatically in all-weather conditions, reducing reliance on highly trained teams and months of preparation
- **Real-Time Adaptive Management**: Implementation of software suite capabilities that can automatically observe wind conditions and adjust flight parameters to ensure adequate battery margin for safe return
- **Mission Planning Automation**: Reduction of manual flight planning burden that previously required months of preparation to account for communication constraints and rugged terrain navigation
- **Routine Capability**: Enabling the same level of operational capability that was demonstrated in Phase II-e to be performed repeatedly and globally without specialized expertise

## Products & Capabilities Described

### Small UAS Platform
- **Demonstrated Capability**: Previously achieved the only visual observations of target volcano during a calendar year during Phase II-e testing
- **Proposed Enhancement**: Automation of mission planning, wind observation, and adaptive flight management
- **Operational Constraint**: Prior missions required very knowledgeable and well-trained teams; proposed solution aims to democratize this capability

## Use Cases & Applications

### Primary Use Case: Volcanic Ash Monitoring
- Data collection for volcanic ash aviation hazards assessment
- In situ atmospheric measurements (wind, temperature) near volcanoes where ground stations are distant or at different elevations
- Validation data for atmospheric dispersion models used in volcanic hazard warnings

### Broader Applications
- Pollution alerts and toxic release response
- Dust storm monitoring
- Wildfire smoke hazard assessment
- General atmospheric model validation in remote/hazardous locations

## Problem Statement & Context
The document emphasizes critical safety implications:
- Existing atmospheric models (weather, dispersion) that inform public safety warnings rely on limited data sources
- Ground systems, crewed aircraft, balloons, and dropsondes have operational limitations
- Satellite data (ASTER, MODIS, AIRS, OMI) suffers from infrequent coverage, cloud masking, poor resolution, and validation gaps
- UAS theoretically can access airspaces too difficult or hazardous for crewed aircraft, but lack of all-weather autonomous capability prevents routine deployment

## Notable Details
- **Phase II-e Achievement**: Demonstrated the only visual observations of target volcano during an entire calendar year, proving concept feasibility
- **Operational Challenge Identified**: Despite proof of concept, the requirement for highly specialized teams and months of preparation severely limited practical deployment
- **Safety Case**: A key barrier to UAS adoption is the ability to automatically conduct missions in all weather conditions with appropriate safety margins
- **Geographic Scope**: Project intended to enable worldwide deployment of routine UAS volcanic monitoring missions
- **Distribution**: Report marked with SBIR Rights Notice (Dec 2007)

## Document Metadata
- Type: Final Report (SF 298 - Report Documentation Page)
- Client/Agency: NASA / Shared Services Center (Stennis Space Center, MS)
- Program/Solicitation: NASA SBIR 2022-1-1118
- Contract Number: 80NSSC22CA192
- Date: 07-08-2024 (report date); 08/09/2024 to 08/07/2024 (dates covered)
- Key Personnel: Jack Elston, Maciej Stachura, Josh Fromm (Black Swift Technologies LLC)
- Performing Organization: Black Swift Technologies LLC, Boulder, CO

## Executive Summary
This is a NASA SBIR final report documenting Black Swift Technologies' work on developing a ruggedized uncrewed aircraft system (UAS) for scientific data collection in harsh environments. The work emphasizes the need for automated flight capabilities in difficult conditions to improve atmospheric model validation and safety systems related to volcanic ash aviation hazards, pollution, and other atmospheric phenomena. Previous Phase II-e work demonstrated small UAS capability for volcano monitoring but revealed that autonomous operation in challenging conditions requires significant automation improvements.

## Technical Approach & Problem Statement
The report identifies a critical gap in UAS operational capability: while instrumented UAS can theoretically operate in airspaces too hazardous for crewed aircraft, the lack of autonomous/automatic operation in all weather conditions limits widespread adoption and safety validation. 

Key issues addressed:
- Current atmospheric models rely on limited ground station data, satellite observations (with gaps from cloud masking, infrequent coverage, resolution limits), and occasional in situ measurements
- Previous volcano monitoring missions required months of planning and real-time wind observation data to ensure safe battery margins and navigation
- Routine hazardous-environment missions require significant human expertise and cannot easily scale worldwide

The proposed solution involves automating much of the flight planning and real-time decision-making that previously required expert human operators.

## Products & Capabilities Described
**Small UAS for Scientific Missions**
- Demonstrated capability during Phase II-e volcano monitoring operations
- Achieved "only visual observations of the target volcano during that calendar year" (implying operational success in conditions that prevented other observation methods)
- Ability to operate in airspaces too difficult or hazardous for crewed aircraft
- Can carry instrumentation for atmospheric science measurements

## Use Cases & Applications
- **Volcano monitoring**: Primary demonstrated use case from Phase II-e; collecting data from volcanic regions
- **Atmospheric model validation**: In situ data collection to improve weather and dispersion models
- **Volcanic ash aviation hazards**: Improving warnings and safety systems
- **Pollution alerts and toxic release monitoring**: Supporting air quality and hazard notification systems
- **Dust storms and wildfire smoke hazards**: Data collection for improved forecasting
- **Wind and temperature measurement**: Basic atmospheric profiling in remote/hazardous locations

## Key Results
- Phase II-e successfully demonstrated small UAS for routine data gathering in harsh volcanic environments
- Achieved unique observational capability during a challenging year when other methods could not obtain visual observations
- Revealed critical need for automation: successful missions required:
  - Months of flight planning and preparation
  - Continuous expert monitoring and wind observation during flight
  - Custom software to manage battery margins and safe return planning
  - Highly trained, knowledgeable flight team

## Notable Details
- **SBIR Rights Notice**: Document includes standard SBIR rights notice (Dec 2007)
- **Atmospheric science focus**: Emphasis on improving model accuracy and validation for safety-critical systems
- **Satellite limitations**: Acknowledges that existing satellite systems (ASTER, MODIS, AIRS, OMI) provide valuable data but have significant constraints
- **Subject classification**: SAR 222 (Same as Report for limitation of abstract)
- **Distribution**: SBIR Rights Notice indicates controlled dissemination

## Document Metadata
- Type: SBIR Phase I Final Report
- Client/Agency: NASA (Shared Services Center, Stennis Space Center, MS)
- Program/Solicitation: NASA SBIR Phase I; Topic A3.02-1718
- Date: 02-02-2024 (report date); Period covered 07/25/2022 to 01/25/2023
- BST Products/Systems Referenced: UAS (uncrewed aircraft system) for atmospheric observation and data collection
- Key Personnel: Jack Elston, Maciej Stachura, Alex Lomis (all BST; phone: 720-638-9656)

## Executive Summary
Black Swift Technologies proposed and executed a pilot study to demonstrate the value of collecting UAS observations near active wildland fires and assimilating that data to improve low-level wind and turbulence forecasting. The work addressed a critical safety gap exposed by a fatal 2021 nighttime air tanker crash potentially caused by low-level turbulence, with the goal of enabling safer and more efficient wildland firefighting operations, including expansion to nighttime operations.

## Technical Approach
- **Observation Collection**: BST would deploy UAS to collect targeted atmospheric observations near wildland fires in complex terrain
- **Data Assimilation**: Partnership with NCAR/RAL to perform data quality assessments and assimilation experiments using an Ensemble Kalman Filter approach specifically tailored to assimilate UAS observations
- **Outcome Metrics**: Quantify improvements in accuracy of low-level winds and turbulence representation; determine critical wind/turbulence criteria required for safe operation of crewed and uncrewed aerial firefighting assets

## Products & Capabilities Described
**Black Swift Technologies UAS**
- Purpose: Collecting low-level atmospheric observations (wind, turbulence) in extreme fire environments
- Application Context: Near active wildland fires in complex terrain where traditional sensors unavailable
- Performance Goal: Provide accurate estimates of current low-level wind field and evolution over 3-12 hour windows

## Use Cases & Applications
- **Wildland Firefighting Operations**: Improved decision support for air tanker operations (both crewed and uncrewed)
- **Nighttime Operations**: Enabling safer nighttime aerial firefighting by providing real-time wind/turbulence data
- **Complex Terrain**: Areas where terrain-induced low-level turbulence poses hazards to conventional firefighting aircraft
- **Extreme Environments**: Operations in high-temperature, smoke-laden, turbulent conditions near active fires

## Partnerships & Collaborations
- **NCAR/RAL (National Center for Atmospheric Research / Research Applications Laboratory)**: Data assimilation and ensemble Kalman filtering expertise
- **Colorado Center of Excellence (CoE) for Advanced Technology Aerial Firefighting**: Coordination of field operations and permissions to collect data near active fires

## Notable Details
- **Triggering Event**: Fatal 2021 air tanker crash during nighttime operations, attributed potentially to strong low-level turbulence—established critical need
- **Safety Focus**: Project explicitly aims to improve safety of mixed (crewed and uncrewed) flight operations in extreme conditions
- **Data Assimilation Innovation**: Ensemble Kalman Filter approach tailored specifically for UAS observations (non-standard for this application)
- **Operational Envelope Expansion**: Goal to extend wildland firefighting operations to nighttime with improved situational awareness
- **Subject Terms**: Wildfire, Extreme Environments, UAS, Earth Science, Wind, Turbulence# SF 298 Form - AFWERX SBIR Phase I Soil Moisture Mapping

## Executive Summary
This document is a template and instruction guide for completing the Standard Form 298 (SF-298), the Report Documentation Page required by the Department of Defense. It provides definitions and guidance for all 19 data fields on the form, which is used to standardize the documentation and metadata for technical reports, research, and project deliverables submitted to government agencies.

## Document Purpose
The SF-298 is a mandatory administrative form used by DoD and other federal agencies to collect standardized metadata about technical reports. The form establishes uniform documentation practices across government-sponsored research and development projects.

## Form Fields & Instructions

1. **Report Date** - Full publication date (DD-MM-YYYY format, Year 2000 compliant)
2. **Report Type** - Category (final, technical, interim, progress, quarterly, etc.)
3. **Dates Covered** - Time period during which work was performed
4. **Title and Subtitle** - Full report title with volume/part numbers if applicable
5. **Identification Numbers** - Contract, grant, program element, project, task, and work unit numbers
6. **Author(s)** - Names of persons responsible for writing/research (format: Last, First, Middle Initial)
7. **Performing Organization** - Name and address of the organization conducting the work
8. **Performing Organization Report Number** - Unique alphanumeric identifier assigned by performing organization
9. **Sponsoring/Monitoring Agency** - Name and address of financially responsible organization
10. **Sponsor/Monitor Acronym(s)** - Agency abbreviations (e.g., BRL, ARDEC, NADC)
11. **Sponsor/Monitor Report Number(s)** - Report identifier assigned by sponsoring agency
12. **Distribution/Availability Statement** - Public availability or distribution restrictions (RD/FRD, PROPIN, ITAR, copyright info)
13. **Supplementary Notes** - Additional information (cooperative arrangements, translations, superseded editions)
14. **Abstract** - Brief factual summary (approximately 200 words) of significant information
15. **Subject Terms** - Keywords or phrases identifying major concepts
16. **Security Classification** - Classification level (U, C, S, etc.) for report, abstract, and page
17. **Limitation of Abstract** - Distribution limitation code (UU = Unclassified Unlimited; SAR = Same as Report)
18. **Number of Pages** - Total page count
19. **Responsible Person Contact** - Name and telephone number of point of contact

## Notable Details
- Public reporting burden estimated at 1 hour per form completion
- Document emphasizes Year 2000 compliance for date fields
- Form prescribed by ANSI Standard Z39.18
- Instructions note that respondents cannot be penalized for non-compliance with collection requirements that lack a valid OMB control number
- Template appears to be part of BST's NASA Autonomy project documentation procedures (based on file location)

## Assessment
This is an administrative reference document with no substantive technical content about BST products, capabilities, or projects. It serves as a procedural guide for completing mandatory federal documentation forms.# SF-298 Template Instructions Document

## Executive Summary
BST proposes the S3, a Group 2 tactical UAS designed for low-altitude persistent monitoring through solar-powered extended endurance (4-6 hours per flight), automated machine vision landing, and terrain-aware flight planning. The system enables month-long automatic monitoring campaigns without extensive pre-planning.

## Technical Approach
The S3 employs several integrated capabilities:
- **Solar power system**: Solar panels integrated on wings for extended flight endurance (4-6 hours per flight)
- **Ground recharging**: Between-flight recharging capability enabling month-long continuous campaigns
- **Automated landing**: Machine vision-based autonomous landing system eliminates need for pre-planned landing zones
- **Terrain-aware flight planning**: On-board elevation models allow low-altitude flight in rugged terrain with terrain-following capability
- **Wind-aware flight planning**: Active wind condition assessment to avoid infeasible flight paths and perform energy harvesting to extend endurance
- **Environmental hardening**: Ingress protection rated for extended temperature range (-40°F to +120°F)

## Products & Capabilities Described

- Classification: Group 2 tactical unmanned aircraft system
- Primary capability: Low-altitude persistent monitoring
- Key features:
  - 4-6 hour endurance per flight with solar power
  - Autonomous machine vision landing
  - Terrain-aware and wind-aware flight planning
  - Rugged environmental protection (-40°F to +120°F operational range)
  - Capable of month-long automated monitoring campaigns

## Use Cases & Applications
- Persistent area monitoring
- Low-altitude surveillance missions
- Long-duration tactical operations in rugged terrain
- Automated monitoring campaigns requiring minimal human intervention

## Notable Details

## Document Metadata
- Type: Technical datasheet / component specification
- Client/Agency: Internal BST reference (NASA SBIR context)
- Program/Solicitation: NASA 2016 SBIR Phase I - Volcano monitoring
- Date: 2016-12-06 to 2016-12-07
- BST Products/Systems Referenced: Not explicitly named; appears to be documentation for integrated pressure sensor component
- Key Personnel: Maciej Stachura (last editor)

## Executive Summary
Technical datasheet for Silicon Microstructures SM9541 pressure sensor series, detailing I2C communication protocols, pin configurations, and product specifications. Document appears to be supporting material for a volcano monitoring application under NASA SBIR Phase I.

## Technical Approach
The document specifies I2C slave communication protocols for a pressure measurement device:
- **Measurement Request (IbC6Read_MR6)**: Slave initiates measurement and DSP calculation cycle
- **Data Fetch Options**:
  - **DF4 (4 bytes)**: Pressure data only
  - **DF8 (8 bytes)**: Pressure data + temperature high byte [hF:8]
  - **DF7 (7 bytes)**: Pressure data + full temperature bytes [hF:8] and [b:F]

All protocols follow standard I2C start/stop conditions with slave addressing [9:F], read/write bit control, ACK/NACK handshakes.

## Products & Capabilities Described

**SM9541 Pressure Sensor Series**
- **Configuration**: Modular product family with designation: SM 9541 [Rated Pressure] [Port Configuration] [Supply Voltage] [Shipping Configuration]
- **Port Configuration**: 
  - C = Vertical Port
  - S = Single-Ended (Dual Ported Gauge)
  - D = Differential
- **Supply Voltage**: 3.3V or 5.0V options
- **Pressure Units**: cmH2O (C), mBar (M), kPa (K), or PSI (default)
- **Shipping Options**: Sticks/Tubes (S) or Tape & Reel (T)
- **Interface**: I2C digital communication
- **Lot Number Format**: 95-00X with tolerance 0.20 +/- 0.10
- **Capacitive Coupling**: 0.1 µF capacitor required in close proximity
- **Pull-up Resistors**: 4.7 kΩ recommended for I2C lines

## Use Cases & Applications
Pressure measurement for volcano monitoring application (implied from file location in NASA SBIR volcano program folder).

## Notable Details
- Silicon Microstructures OEM component integrated into BST system
- Dual communication protocol options allow flexibility in data retrieval (pressure only vs. pressure + temperature)
- Decoupling capacitor and pull-up resistor requirements specified for proper I2C bus operation
- Document references "Silicon Microstructures Warranty and Disclaimer" (text cut off)
- Bit-level I2C protocol documentation suggests integration into custom firmware/DSP processing# Small UAS Question

## Document Metadata
- **Type:** SBIR Phase I Proposal
- **Client/Agency:** U.S. Air Force
- **Program/Solicitation:** SBIR Topic AF192-005
- **Proposal Number:** F192-006-1065
- **Date:** Submitted 2019 (created June 26, 2019; modified November 1, 2019)
- **BST Products/Systems Referenced:** S2 UAS, Soil Moisture Mapping (SMM) UAS
- **Key Personnel:** Dr. Jack Elston (Principal Investigator, Founder and CEO)

## Executive Summary
Black Swift Technologies proposes to modify its existing Soil Moisture Mapping (SMM) UAS—developed in partnership with NASA for precision agriculture and scientific research—for Air Force applications. The system uses a high-resolution L-band radiometer to provide soil moisture maps at 15-meter spatial resolution down to ~10 cm depth. Phase I would establish specific Air Force customer needs, develop integration plans with Air Force weather models (particularly WRF), and document required modifications for deployment to support trafficability forecasts and runway operations.

## Technical Approach

**System Overview:**
- L-band radiometer mounted on BST's S2 UAS platform
- Provides local soil moisture measurements at 15-meter spatial resolution to ~10 cm depth
- Currently developed under NASA SBIR contract in collaboration with University of Colorado's Center for Environmental Technology (CET)
- System has been flight-tested at NASA SMAP calibration sites and commercial agriculture research farms with validation against in situ sensors

**Phase I Strategy:**
1. **Kickoff Meeting:** Establish contacts and map strategy with Air Force technical monitor
2. **Preliminary Integration Plan:** Collaborate with NOAA experts (Mimi Hughes, Rob Cifelli, Kelly Mahoney) and Professor Dev Niyogi (Purdue) to develop detailed WRF model integration plan
3. **Customer Discovery:** Reach out to 3 DoD end users to identify specific needs, focusing on Air Force forecast models and trafficability applications
4. **Requirements Documentation:** Document DoD user requirements and identify necessary instrument, CONOPS, and data structure modifications
5. **Integration Study:** Conduct detailed technical analysis to answer key questions about required resolution, accuracy, area coverage, data frequency, and format/interface requirements for seamless Air Force system integration
6. **Final Report:** Deliver comprehensive documentation for Phase II transition

**Key Research Questions to Address:**
- What resolution, accuracy, and area coverage is needed for meaningful WRF model contribution?
- What frequency and spatial coverage are required for sufficient Air Force user value?
- What are specific interfacing and format requirements for integration with existing Air Force systems?

## Products & Capabilities Described

### Soil Moisture Mapping (SMM) UAS
- **What it is:** Small unmanned aircraft system equipped with high-resolution L-band radiometer
- **Specifications:** 
  - 15-meter spatial resolution
  - ~10 cm soil moisture measurement depth
  - Lightweight airborne platform
  - On-demand, local measurement capability
- **Current Applications:** Precision agriculture, hydrological scientific studies, weather research
- **Proposed Air Force Applications:**
  - Integration into Air Force weather modeling (WRF)
  - Aircraft operations on unimproved runways (soil integrity assessment)
  - Army trafficability support
  - Battlefield environment characterization

### S2 UAS
- Airframe platform carrying the L-band radiometer payload
- Avionics developed by Dr. Elston with EMI reduction for measurement quality
- Interfaces with multiple sensors for soil moisture determination
- Flight control enabling safe near-ground operations
- Pilot-in-command operations demonstrated

## Use Cases & Applications

**Air Force:**
- Support for Air Force weather forecasts and climate analysis
- Aircraft operations on unimproved runways—soil integrity assessment for landing safety
- Integration with 557th Weather Wing (primary target customer)
- Support for both Air Force and Army weather requirements

**Army:**
- Trafficability forecasting (identified as top Army priority)
- Augmentation of existing Air Force weather data products

**Longer-term/Dual-use Applications:**
- Persistent theater soil moisture imagery via high altitude platform adaptation
- FEMA flash flood prediction (demonstrated in 2007 with older instrument version in North Texas/Oklahoma)
- Precision agriculture commercialization

**Competitive Advantage vs. Alternatives:**
- **vs. In situ probes:** Point-only measurements requiring considerable redeployment effort
- **vs. Satellites (SMAP):** Provides much higher spatial resolution (~15m vs. satellite coarse resolution) and on-demand capability vs. fixed satellite measurement cycles

## Notable Details

**Partnership & Development History:**
- 5-year development partnership with University of Colorado's Center for Environmental Technology (CET)
- Flight-tested at NASA SMAP calibration site with extensive in situ sensor validation
- Developed under existing NASA SBIR contract
- System is ready for DoD field application with reduced technical risk

**Commercialization Strategy:**
- Primary target: 557th Weather Wing (Air Force)
- Dual-use approach: Continue precision agriculture commercialization to keep DoD price points competitive
- Expansion potential to NOAA, National Weather Service

## Document Metadata
- Type: Product/capability datasheet
- Client/Agency: Center for Environmental Technology (CET); Colorado Advanced Industries
- Program/Solicitation: NASA SBIR (sUAS integration phase)
- Date: March 2, 2015
- BST Products/Systems Referenced: SwiftCore, SwiftPilot, SwiftStation, SwiftTab, SuperSwift aircraft platform
- Key Personnel: Dr. Al Gasiewski (collaboration partner mentioned); team with 30+ years sUAS experience noted

## Executive Summary
Black Swift Technologies offers an integrated soil moisture mapping sUAS combining a passive L-band microwave radiometer with their SwiftCore avionics system to provide volumetric soil moisture measurements at 15m resolution and 5-20cm depth. The hand-launched system covers 1-2 km² per hour and is available as a turnkey solution with existing FAA and NASA approvals for U.S. operations.

## Technical Approach
The system integrates a calibrated passive L-band microwave radiometer sensor with:
- Precision GPS (10 Hz, raw measurements, <1m accuracy)
- High-rate IMU (100 Hz attitude updates, 9 DOF, 1 kHz sampling)
- Differential and static pressure sensing
- NDVI sensor (near-infrared and red wavelength, nadir and zenith)
- Thermal imaging (surface temperature)

Flight control via SwiftCore avionics provides real-time telemetry (10 Hz) through tablet/mobile interface (Swift Tab), enabling precision low-altitude operations for accurate soil moisture mapping.

## Products & Capabilities Described

### SwiftCore™ Flight Management System
- Integrated avionics solution consisting of SwiftPilot, SwiftStation, and SwiftTab
- Designed specifically for small UAS (<50 lbs)
- Fully customizable and field-tested in FAA-approved operations
- Includes guide for FAA COA applications

### SwiftPilot™
- 50-gram flight management autopilot
- Dimensions: 6.7 × 4.0 × 1.8 cm
- Dual 168 MHz Cortex-M4 processors with FPU
- Multiple interfaces: CAN, UART, I2C, SPI, Ethernet, USB, GPIO
- Gumstix Overo (1 GHz Cortex-A8) onboard payload computer for customer use
- Included software SDK

### SwiftTab™
- Mobile ground control station (tablet/phone form factor)
- Android-based with gesture and multi-touch interface
- 10 Hz telemetry reception

### SuperSwift™ Aircraft Platform
- Empty weight: 3.4 kg
- Nominal payload capacity: 1.4 kg (maximum 2 kg)
- Cruise speed: 18 m/s
- Maximum speed: 25 m/s
- Endurance: 90 minutes with payload
- Range: 100 km maximum; 10 km standard communication range
- Features: Hand-launch, laser-guided autoland, operations from unimproved surfaces
- Full autonomous capability
- Custom nose cone available up to 65 cm length for payload accommodation
- Field-swappable payload nose cone

### Soil Moisture Sensor Suite
- **L-band Microwave Radiometer**: Passive measurement at 15m resolution from 15m altitude; penetration depth 5-20 cm
- **NDVI Sensor**: Nadir and zenith measurement of near-infrared and red wavelengths
- **Thermal Imaging**: Surface temperature measurement

## Use Cases & Applications
- Agricultural soil moisture mapping without infrastructure requirements
- Scientific Cal/Val (calibration/validation) bridge between manned aviation and in situ sensors
- Data collection over difficult terrain and high-variance areas
- Agricultural plot-scale operations

## Coverage Performance
- **15m resolution**: 1 km² (247 acres) per hour
- **30m resolution**: 2 km² (494 acres) per hour

## Operational Status & Availability
- Existing FAA and NASA approvals for U.S. operations
- Data collection service available through experienced team (30+ years sUAS experience as of April 2015)
- Turnkey system availability planned for Fall 2015
- Sole-source acquisition available through existing contract mechanism
